## Geometry Is Part of the Machine {#sec-lay-ch04}

## A Concrete Picture

Push a door near its hinge, then with the same force near its handle. The
turning effect changes because the force has a different moment arm. Push
directly toward the hinge and the moment about that hinge is zero in the ideal
model. Your hand can still exert force and load the structure. Moment, force,
motion, and effort are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A swing has several moving versions of this geometry. Joint axes, hand
positions, club orientation, and shaft deformation change how forces map into
moments and how commanded torques produce acceleration. The useful question is
not whether one posture has more “leverage” in general. It is leverage for
which motion or force, about which reference, under which constraints.

![The Moment Arm Is the Perpendicular Distance From O to the Force's Line of Action.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_moment_arm_geometry.svg){#fig-lay-moment-arm width=95% fig-alt="Two equal-magnitude force arrows act at H on a straight club. A dashed line extends each force's line of action; the green segment from reference O meets it perpendicularly. Changing force direction changes that distance and the moment about O."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Name the Point, Plane, and Direction

For a force on the club applied at point $H$, its moment about $O$ is

$$
\mathbf M_O=(\mathbf r_H-\mathbf r_O)\times\mathbf F.
$$

This instantaneous definition does not require $O$ to be fixed or inertial.
Using that moment in an angular-momentum balance about a moving point requires
the appropriate transport terms; the definition alone is not that balance.
An additional applied free moment must be included separately.

The magnitude of a point-force moment about $O$ is force magnitude times the
perpendicular distance from $O$ to its line of action. It is not generally the distance
to the arrow tip, the contact point, or the end of the club. A 100 N force with
a 0.04 m perpendicular moment arm gives 4 N m. Doubling that distance at the
same force gives 8 N m. Passing the line through $O$ gives exactly zero.

For a planar idealization, let $\mathbf n$ be the declared unit normal to the
plane, let the unit vector $\mathbf e_r$ point along the straight club, and define the
**in-plane** transverse direction $\mathbf e_t=\mathbf n\times\mathbf e_r$.
The transverse direction is not the normal to the swing plane. If the force
and club lie in the plane, write $\mathbf F=F_r\mathbf e_r+F_t\mathbf e_t$.
When $\mathbf r_H-\mathbf r_O=\ell\mathbf e_r$, the signed moment about
$\mathbf n$ is $\ell F_t$. The signed distance $\ell$ matters: changing which
side of $O$ contains the contact can change the sign.

The radial term has zero moment under those collinearity assumptions. It can
nevertheless accelerate the club center, load the shaft, or transfer power
when the contact moves along its force. A curved shaft, an offset reference,
or an out-of-plane force needs the full geometry. “Radial” alone does not
specify a zero moment about every point.

### Changing the Reference Preserves a Contract, Not Every Number

A wrench combines resultant force $\mathbf R$ and total moment about a declared
point. Moving the reference from $A$ to $B$, with
$\mathbf d=\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A$, gives

$$
\mathbf M_B=\mathbf M_A-\mathbf d\times\mathbf R.
$$

A pure couple has $\mathbf R=0$ and the same moment about every point. For a
nearly opposed force pair, the moment change is bounded by
$\lVert\mathbf d\rVert\lVert\mathbf R\rVert$. A small resultant supports a
small-change claim only with a bounded reference displacement and a stated
tolerance. It does not make a nonzero-resultant wrench a pure couple.

Power provides a second check. On a rigid body, use the velocity of the same
reference point as the moment:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf v_A+\mathbf M_A\cdot\boldsymbol\omega,\\
\mathbf v_B&=\mathbf v_A+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf d.
\end{aligned}
$$

Transporting both moment and velocity leaves $P$ unchanged. Transporting only
one creates a false power difference. For a deforming shaft or distributed
contact, a single rigid-body twist need not describe every loaded point;
retain the individual force–velocity pairings or the corresponding distributed
power integral.

Expressing the same vectors in another orthonormal basis changes their
components while preserving dot products. Changing the physical observer is
a different operation: an observer translating at velocity $\mathbf U$
measures force power shifted by $-\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf U$ when the same
physical forces are used. Wrenches and trajectories have transformation rules;
their component lists are not universally frame-invariant observables. The
[Modern Robotics wrench discussion](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/3-4-wrenches/)
develops the paired force/motion representation.

### The Jacobian Maps Velocities and Their Dual Forces

Suppose a hand position is $\mathbf x_H=\mathbf f(\mathbf q,t)$. Differentiating
gives a velocity contribution from the modeled coordinates and another from
any explicit prescribed motion:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v_H&=\mathbf J_H\dot{\mathbf q}+\mathbf b_H,\\
\mathbf J_H&=\partial\mathbf f/\partial\mathbf q,\qquad
\mathbf b_H=\partial\mathbf f/\partial t,\\
\mathbf Q_H&=\mathbf J_H^{\mathsf T}\mathbf F_H.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\mathbf F_H$ acts on the modeled hand. The force that hand exerts on the
club has the opposite sign; choose the system before applying the mapping.
The last line maps this applied force into generalized force; it does not
assert static equilibrium or identify the total actuator torque. Force and
Jacobian must use compatible components and the same point. Generalized force
is a torque for an angular coordinate and a force for a length coordinate;
its units and components change with coordinate scaling.

The power identity is
$\mathbf F_H\cdot\mathbf v_H=\mathbf Q_H\cdot\dot{\mathbf q}
+\mathbf F_H\cdot\mathbf b_H$. Ignoring the last term can hide the power
associated with prescribed base motion. If base coordinates are included in
the dynamical system instead, their rates and generalized forces belong in the
larger mapping. A force-plus-free-moment contact uses the corresponding linear
and angular velocity Jacobians.

Coordinate derivatives are not always the software's generalized speeds.
Quaternion orientation, for example, uses four constrained coordinates but
three rotational speed components. Write $\dot{\mathbf q}=\mathbf N(\mathbf q)
\boldsymbol\nu$ and use $\mathbf J_H\mathbf N$ when mapping those speeds.
The dual generalized force is then $\mathbf N^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Q_H$.
[Tedrake's multibody notes](https://underactuated.mit.edu/multibody.html)
explain this distinction. Neither a particular coordinate count nor a matrix
entry by itself identifies an anatomical actuator.

### Near a Singularity, Motion and Force Have Different Scalings

A Jacobian becomes singular for its declared task when its rank falls below
the maximum attainable rank. A robot with fewer joints than task dimensions
can already lack some instantaneous motions without being at a special
singular posture. Instantaneous inability to move in one direction also does
not prove that a finite path to another configuration is impossible.

Consider a dimensionless, consistently scaled example
$\mathbf J=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon>0$.
Unit task velocity in the second direction requires joint rate
$1/\varepsilon$ in that direction. But a specified task-force component of
10 gives generalized force $10\varepsilon$, not $10/\varepsilon$.
Conversely, solving for task force from a fixed generalized force gives
$1/\varepsilon$ scaling under this ideal invertible mapping.

At $\varepsilon=0$, no finite joint rate gives the missing task velocity,
while that task-force component contributes zero generalized force. Its
magnitude is therefore not determined by joint torque through this mapping.
Structure, contact, compliance, strength limits, and dynamics still matter;
the equation does not grant unlimited physical force or independent force
control. The
[Modern Robotics singularity examples](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/5-3-singularities/)
illustrate the difference between active motion and structural force support.

For multiple coordinates, the analogous statements apply along singular-vector
directions with declared units and scaling. Distinguish motions in the
Jacobian's nullspace from force components in the transpose nullspace. Neither
algebraic ambiguity alone proves that a biological force is unidentifiable
from every possible sensor, dynamical model, and experiment.

### Inertia Couples the Response Through the Equations of Motion

In independent coordinates, a reduced equation can be written
$\mathbf M(\mathbf q)\ddot{\mathbf q}+\mathbf h=\mathbf Q$.
At fixed state and fixed non-control terms, the acceleration change is
$\delta\ddot{\mathbf q}=\mathbf M^{-1}\delta\mathbf Q$.
It is the inverse mapping, not one off-diagonal mass entry alone, that answers
which coordinate accelerates under an added generalized force.

For example, in consistent normalized units, let
$\mathbf M=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]$.
An added force vector $(1,0)$ gives acceleration change $(2/3,-1/3)$.
The off-diagonal mass entry is positive while the cross-acceleration response
is negative. A linear coordinate transformation can diagonalize this matrix;
transforming the force and reconstructing the motion gives the same physical
response. Removing an off-diagonal entry by relabeling coordinates does not
remove the original endpoint response.

In a constrained two-hand model, admissible acceleration changes also satisfy
the linearized acceleration constraint at the fixed state. Reactions change
with the command, so solve the coupled constrained equations or use a valid
reduced-coordinate model. Applying an unconstrained inverse mass matrix and
ignoring the changed reactions answers another question. Near a constraint-rank
change, check the solve's validity before interpreting large numerical values.

Posture affects these mappings, while velocity affects the remaining dynamics.
A same-state control comparison holds both fixed. Comparing club angles is a
comparison across different configurations, each with its own same-state
allocation experiment; it is not one unchanged state with several angles.

### A Two-Hand Couple Has Exact, Conditional Controls

Let the contact separation be $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_T-\mathbf r_L$.
If the trail contact applies $+\mathbf F$ and the lead contact applies
$-\mathbf F$, the resultant is zero and the couple is exactly
$\mathbf d\times\mathbf F$. Its magnitude is $dF$ only when the vectors are
perpendicular. Collapsing separation or making $\mathbf F$ parallel to $\mathbf d$ removes
this point-force couple. Applied free moments can remain.

Reversing the force with the separation held fixed reverses the couple.
Reversing the separation while retaining the same force assignment also
reverses it. Rigidly rotating the entire force system rotates its moment;
it does not necessarily reverse a consistently transformed scalar component.
Merely swapping contact labels changes no physical force system at all.

For arbitrary forces, define the common component
$\mathbf F_c=(\mathbf F_L+\mathbf F_T)/2$ and differential component
$\mathbf F_d=(\mathbf F_L-\mathbf F_T)/2$. The resultant is $2\mathbf F_c$,
and the point-force moment about the midpoint is
$-\mathbf d\times\mathbf F_d$. For the pure pair above, $\mathbf F_d=-\mathbf F$,
recovering the same positive $\mathbf d\times\mathbf F$ expression.
A common component can contribute a moment
about another reference. Direct free moments must still be added. This
decomposition is useful bookkeeping, not a measurement of separate muscles.

These geometric controls require declared held-fixed forces. If changing grip
separation also changes solved reactions, the resulting couple need not scale
linearly with separation. A measured or simulated reversal test must report
both the changed geometry and force response. Otherwise a failed simple
scaling law need not be a failed cross-product implementation.

### What the Allocation Study Actually Holds Fixed

The pinned provider uses a planar rigid-club model with two constrained arms.
At each of 19 club angles from $-12^\circ$ to $24^\circ$, it constructs a
constraint-consistent configuration with club center at $(0,-0.50)$ m and
zero generalized velocity. This is an instantaneous dynamical comparison;
zero initial velocity does not imply static equilibrium.

For each configuration it evaluates commanded and zero-command dynamics at
the same state, then subtracts them. The fixed task is the club's rotational inertia times
the **control-only angular-acceleration difference**, set to 8 N m. It is not
the full net wrench, every acceleration component, or a complete trajectory.
The force resultant is allowed to change.

One control subspace uses four shoulder/elbow torques with both wrist commands
zero; another uses the two wrist torques with proximal commands zero. In each,
the implementation chooses the minimum unweighted Euclidean norm of actuator
commands that satisfies the scalar task. It blends these two normalized
controls, scaled to the common task, at 21 fractions from zero to one. Linearity of the fixed-state
constrained solve preserves the scalar task across that blend; it is not a
general superposition claim for finite nonlinear swings.

The blending fraction is **not** the fraction of net club moment supplied by
direct wrist moments. At the wrist-only endpoint, direct moments sum to about
8.13–10.02 N m across the angles; opposing contact-force moments bring the
control-only total back to 8 N m. The archive's variable called a grip-force
“couple” is the contact-force moment about the club center. With a nonzero
resultant, it need not be a pure couple of equal opposite forces.

The reported hand-force RMS is the root mean square of the two **control-only
force-vector norms at that instant**. It is not a time RMS or the norm of total
physical contact loads. A control-only force is the difference between two
same-state solutions; the norm of that difference is not the difference of
their norms. The torque metric is the unweighted norm of six actuator commands,
not muscle force, metabolic cost, tissue loading, work, or a coordinate-free
measure of effort.

Independent recomputation of the archived arrays reproduces the scalar task
and moment closure with residuals below $6\times10^{-15}$ N m. The hand-force metric
ranges from 7.58 to 91.51 N and the torque norm from 5.74 to 25.45 N m.
Among the sampled blend fractions, hand-force minima occur from 0.75 to 0.90,
whereas torque-norm minima occur from 0.85 to 0.95, depending on angle.
These are grid minima along one restricted blend of two subspace solutions.
They do not establish global optima over every admissible allocation, a
physiological optimum, or an optimal human grip. Archived summaries were
recomputed; the constrained model was not rerun for this chapter review.

### Connect Geometry to the Question Being Tested

Geometry, inertia, actuation, constraints, and objectives enter the same chain
of reasoning. Geometry maps contact motion and forces; inertia and constraints
determine acceleration response; a chosen objective prices the resulting
delivery and internal demands. Changing one of these can change a preferred
allocation without proving that the original physical mechanism was absent.

For a geometry hypothesis, first declare the system, reference, coordinates,
contact model, and task. Then distinguish a bookkeeping transformation from a
physical intervention. Check algebraic identities at fixed forces, and report
the dynamically recomputed forces for changed geometry. Finally evaluate the
outcomes and constraints that matter to the proposed use. Chapter 3 explains
state matching, Chapters 9–10 connect force to work, and Chapter 23 treats
uncertainty and competing objectives.

Human motion and contact are more complicated than this planar illustration.
Kinematic measurements can describe geometry, but they do not alone select the
bilateral force allocation that produced it. McPhee's review provides context
for the range and limitations of golf models [@mcphee2022]; it is not direct
validation of this allocation surface or a technique prescription.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The door has a fixed hinge; the golfer, compliant grip, and shaft do not reduce
to that single joint. A contact's moment about one point is not automatically
its contribution to every generalized acceleration. Likewise, favorable
force transmission in one direction can coincide with poor velocity authority,
limited motion range, or unacceptable loading.

**Model Result:** The archived reduced model admits different actuator blends
with the same scalar control-moment task and different internal metrics.
Geometry changes the preferred sampled blend for each declared metric.

**Measurement Boundary:** Coordinate-consistent wrenches and motion are needed
to compare physical actions. Independent information is needed to constrain
individual hand forces and biological actuator allocation; small numerical
closure residuals supply no human validation.

**Hypothesis:** An opposing club-moment component can arise from two-hand force
geometry. Whether it persists or improves delivery under a changed grip must
be tested with the changed reactions and full dynamical state, not inferred
from one negative projection.

**Practical Interpretation:** Ask where the force acts, which direction it
points, what motion it accompanies, and which task it helps accomplish. Those
questions turn a vague claim about leverage into a comparison that can fail.
